query: For high-entropy alloys intended as intermediate materials in plasma-facing reactor components, what single intervention could improve heat-transfer capability while preserving structural integrity? Formulate one hypothesis specifying the intervention, its mechanism, the expected outcome compared with current intermediate-layer performance, the temperature and loading conditions under which it should hold, supporting prior evidence, and a controlled experiment that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: Introducing 5 at.% copper into a refractory high-entropy alloy (HEA) of nominal composition W₀.₂Ta₀.₂Mo₀.₂Nb₀.₂V₀.₂ (atomic fractions) by laser-directed energy deposition will generate an interconnected Cu-rich nanophase along interdendritic regions that raises the effective electron-dominated thermal conductivity of the intermediate layer by ≈30 % while retaining ≥90 % of its baseline 800 °C yield strength.
generation.material_initial_state: Vacuum-arc-melted, equiatomic WTaMoNbV HEA plate (≈25 W m⁻¹ K⁻¹ at 800 °C, yield strength ≈1.0 GPa at 800 °C); grain size ≈20 µm; single BCC solid solution; porosity <1 %.
generation.intervention: Add 5 at.% Cu powder to the feedstock and fabricate the layer by laser-directed energy deposition (L-DED) using a melt-pool dwell time <2 ms to limit Cu evaporation, followed by a 1200 °C/1 h stress-relief anneal in vacuum.
generation.conditions: Steady-state heat flux 5–15 MW m⁻²; bulk temperatures 600–1000 °C; uniaxial tensile stresses ≤150 MPa; high-vacuum (≤10⁻⁴ Pa) helium plasma exposure up to 10²⁶ m⁻² ion fluence.
generation.structural_mediator: A percolating network of ~50–200 nm Cu-rich precipitates decorating prior‐dendrite boundaries within the BCC refractory matrix.
generation.mechanism: 1) The high electron mobility of the Cu-rich network supplies parallel, low-resistance pathways for heat, lowering interfacial thermal resistance and boosting overall conductivity; 2) coherent Cu/BCC interfaces and nanoscale precipitate spacing impede dislocation motion (Orowan strengthening) compensating soft Cu addition, so macroscopic yield strength remains largely unchanged; 3) the ductile Cu network blunts crack tips and relaxes thermal stresses, preserving structural integrity under cyclic heating.
generation.predicted_outcome: Effective thermal conductivity k(800 °C) increases from ~25 W m⁻¹ K⁻¹ (baseline) to ~32 ± 3 W m⁻¹ K⁻¹; 0.2 % proof stress at 800 °C remains ≥0.9 GPa (≤10 % reduction). Fatigue life under ±100 MPa at 800 °C is unchanged or slightly improved by crack blunting.
generation.baseline: Same alloy processed by identical L-DED schedule but without Cu addition.
generation.boundary: Benefits diminish if Cu content exceeds 7 at.% (coarsening and softening) or service temperature exceeds 1100 °C (Cu network coalescence and liquation).
generation.uncertainty: No published data yet on Cu-modified refractory HEAs under fusion-relevant heat flux; magnitude of conductivity boost is extrapolated from mixture rules and similar nanocomposite studies. Possible Cu segregation under prolonged neutron irradiation remains unknown.

falsification_experiment.design: Produce two 3 mm-thick L-DED walls: (A) WTaMoNbV (baseline) and (B) WTaMoNbV-5Cu (intervention). Characterise as-built and post-anneal microstructures by SEM/TEM/EDS to confirm Cu network. Measure thermal diffusivity (laser flash) from 25 – 1000 °C and calculate k. Machine tensile specimens and test at 800 °C. Finally, expose both materials to 10 MW m⁻² electron beam pulses (10⁴ cycles) and evaluate surface cracking.
measurements: 0.2 % proof stress and ultimate tensile strength at 800 °C
Fatigue crack initiation cycles under ±100 MPa at 800 °C
Microstructure before/after testing (network continuity, precipitate size)
Surface crack density after thermal cycling
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: Hypothesis is falsified if: (i) k(800 °C) of sample B is ≤10 % higher than sample A, OR (ii) yield strength of sample B at 800 °C is <0.85 × that of sample A, OR (iii) sample B exhibits ≥20 % higher surface crack density than sample A after thermal cycling.
